newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to tackle deficit without stifling growth.
newsitem.headline: France to tackle deficit without stifling growth.

text.p: French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, drawing demarcation lines in a stand-off with Germany over monetary union, said on Thursday any moves to curb the public deficit must not stifle economic growth.
In his first television interview since taking office a month ago, Jospin reiterated that his Socialist-led government was committed to a single European currency.
If an independent audit of public finances due on July 21 showed the deficit significantly overshooting, measures would be taken to curb it, he said.
Jospin declined to say what level of deficit he considered acceptable to meet the Maastricht treaty criteria limiting it to three percent of gross domestic product.
"We must curb public spending without stifling growth," he said, adding that unemployment must also be brought down.
His comments echoed those made earlier by Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn who said the government must take account of the needs of the French economy.
"The target will be defined according to what the economy can bear," Strauss-Kahn told a news conference. "We have to be able to reduce this deficit by a few decimal points."
Analysts suggest this year's public deficit could be between 3.4 and 3.8 percent of GDP, and forecast government action to bring it to a more acceptable level of around 3.3 percent.
Even that would leave France at odds with Germany, its main ally in monetary union, which is aiming for exactly 3.0 percent of GDP to ensure a strict reading of the treaty.
Strauss-Kahn said the audit of public finances could show a French deficit significantly higher than 3.0 percent, and there were grounds to fear it would be more than 3.4 percent.
The government has insisted that Maastricht criteria should be interpreted in terms of trend rather than precise numbers.
"We have always said we must apply the treaty, the whole treaty and nothing but the treaty," Strauss-Kahn said. "It is clear some people can have different readings of the treaty."

Jospin promised in the election campaign which swept his rainbow coalition to office in an upset victory on June 1 that he would not impose new austerity just to meet a strict interpretation of the treaty.

In a veiled swipe at Germany on Thursday, he said it suited some European Union countries to stress only the deficit level but all the criteria in the Maastricht treaty must be considered when deciding in April/May 1998 which states qualify to join a single currency in 1999.
One of those conditions requires debt to be reduced to 60 percent of GDP, a target Germany is likely to miss.
The divergence between Paris and Bonn over interpreting Maastricht is only one of a range of disputes between the two countries on the future shape of monetary union.
They also disagree on the degree of political coordination needed among countries inside the euro zone.
Jospin repeated that political coordination, which France says must focus on boosting growth and jobs, was essential. "Europe cannot be reduced to a market, or a currency," he said.
Germany fears any attempt by politicians to influence the exchange rate of the new euro which would undermine the independence of the future European Central Bank.
